dimensions.name: Contract & semantics reverse-engineering

evidence.note: Explicitly framed the work as reverse-engineering the contract: 'inspect the first-party helper to pin down the exact API shape before implementing' — orientation as deliberate strategy, not incidental.
Read helpers.py, run.sh in full, extracting the REST envelope (list_workbooks['workbooks'], create returns id, patch body shape) directly from client code.

Systematically read EVERY public test file plus conftest before committing to a design — engine, deps, spill, copy/fill, sort/filter, csv, xlsx, collab, ooxml, iter, pivot, locale, validation, oracle. This is the full-client-surface contract inventory described in the level-8 anchor.

Cross-checked ambiguous shapes against actual assertions: spill anchor fields (spill:true, spill_range:{rows,cols}), collab welcome/event/presence payloads, locale separators (SUMME(A1;A2)) — grounded rather than guessed.
During build, inspected the LibreOffice oracle .xlsx fixtures via openpyxl as ground truth to diagnose aggregate-flattening semantics — evidence-based re-derivation of Excel behavior.

Semantic fixes (INDEX over 1-col range, aggregate arg flattening, pivot count) were driven reactively by smoke-test failures rather than deliberate pre-emptive edge probing — the ceiling that keeps this below level 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent front-loaded a systematic, complete mapping of the client surface — helpers.py, run.sh, and all ~15 public test files — before committing to a design, and cross-checked genuinely ambiguous shapes (spill anchor fields, collab payloads, locale separators) against actual client assertions, matching the level-8 anchor. It also grounded xlsx/aggregate semantics against the LibreOffice oracle fixtures via openpyxl. It falls short of 10 because most mid-build semantic corrections were reactive to smoke-test failures rather than deliberate ambiguity resolution via stubs, and orientation was heavily front-loaded rather than a sustained evidence-driven re-derivation.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone checkpoints

evidence.note: Opening prose states intent to pin the contract first and identifies the broad subsystem slice (engine, spills, collab, csv/xlsx, validation, formatting, pivots, locale) — foundational-first instinct, but no explicit ordered milestone plan with per-item done-criteria is written.

Architectural sequencing (launcher before app, JSON store, persist-per-mutation) but the entire app across all ~15 subsystems was written in a single monolithic 63KB apply_patch rather than built as sequenced milestones.

Verification run in chunks with a sensible foundational-first ordering: api/engine/deps first, then spills/copy/sort/csv, then xlsx/ooxml/iter/pivot/locale/validation — rough milestones tied to getting dev_tests chunks green.

Foundational recompute/aggregate correctness bugs (INDEX, SUM flattening) surfaced only after the whole app was built, showing build-all-then-fix rather than nailing foundational correctness before layering features.
Full suite green plus an explicit manual persistence-restart done-check (create workbook, write formula, stop/start, re-read B1=42) — a concrete verification hook for the persistence milestone.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed a sensible foundational-first orientation and used concrete done-checks (health endpoint, chunked test passes ordered core→dependent, an explicit persistence restart check), which exceeds a flat unordered to-do list (anchor 3). But it never produced an explicit dependency-aware milestone decomposition of the ~15 subsystems; instead it built everything in one monolithic patch and discovered foundational dependency/aggregate bugs only afterward, so it did not 'nail foundational correctness before layering' as anchor 8 requires. The ordering that exists is mostly in verification chunks tied to dev_tests going green, matching anchor 5 with a slight lean toward 6 for the concrete verification hooks.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification beyond the smoke suite

evidence.note: Ran dev_tests/run.sh repeatedly in feature chunks as the primary verification loop, ending on '131 passed'; the smoke suite is the backbone of its checking (anchor 3 behavior).

Added ad-hoc debug scripts tied to specific failures: reproducing the INDEX bug, reading the aggregates.xlsx fixture with openpyxl, and a curl xlsx-import probe for pivot — spot-checks of features it built (anchor 5 behavior), but debugging-oriented rather than independent oracle tests.
Self-built restart-persistence check beyond the suite: wrote =A1+1, stopped/restarted the process, confirmed B1=42 persisted — a deliberate check it constructed, pushing above pure anchor 5.

Final report cites only 'run.sh passes' plus the manual restart check as verification — no performance timing, no self-built xlsx round-trip fidelity, no spill/ghost-write rejection or formula known-answer tables.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent leaned on the smoke suite as its main verification (anchor 3), supplemented by ad-hoc feature spot-checks and openpyxl fixture inspection (anchor 5), and added one genuinely self-built check — restart persistence (73-79) — that goes beyond what was handed to it. But it never built the broader targeted battery anchor 8 describes: no independent xlsx round-trip fidelity test of its own export, no formula known-answer tables, no spill/ghost-write rejection self-test, and no performance benchmarking against the stated envelopes. That places it solidly between the 5 and 8 anchors, i.e. a 6.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the surface

evidence.note: Read all 14 dev_test files upfront, inventorying the full subsystem surface before coding — establishes an accurate initial map of what must be built.
Explicitly enumerated the required subsystem slice (formula eval, spills, WebSocket, CSV/XLSX, validation, formatting, pivots, locale), showing a concrete done-vs-remaining frame.
Ran the visible suite in subsystem-grouped chunks, using the test files as a coverage checklist to localize which areas were green vs pending (79/1, then 88, then 22/2, then full 131 passed).
Prose reconciles completed vs pending subsystems ('formula/spills/CSV passing now; moving to XLSX, OOXML, iterative calc, pivot, locale, validation, collab') — a running status that is followed.
Debugging arc (INDEX, aggregate oracle, pivot count) was targeted and root-caused without circling on any one area — no evidence of stuck re-debugging.
Reconciled claimed-done against verified-done: full-suite pass plus a separate manual persistence restart check beyond the chunk runs.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept an accurate, followed running picture of completed vs pending subsystems — inventorying the surface upfront and using subsystem-grouped test chunks as a live coverage map — and never lost the plot, abandoned, or repeated work (anchor 5, comfortably). It edged toward anchor 8 by reconciling verified-done against claimed-done (full suite + separate persistence check) and by localizing failures precisely so debugging never circled. It falls short of 8 because tracking relied on the external visible suite rather than an explicit self-maintained per-subsystem/function ledger, and there was no conscious time-boxing or breadth-reallocation, so I place it at 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: Committed to core bets (FastAPI, single JSON store, in-memory dirty recompute, openpyxl) with no validating probe of risky assumptions — especially no performance test of the 100k-cell / 5000-dependent targets. Bets made, not de-risked.

INDEX returning #NAME? diagnosed to root cause (arg list treated as matrix during error scan) and fixed at the responsible evaluator path with a recursive contains_error helper — reactive but correct component-level fix.

Aggregate oracle failure traced to arg-list flattening in the evaluator; added recursive flatten_values. A modest structural rework of the evaluator, triggered by a failing test rather than anticipated.
Pivot 'count' crash fixed by replacing eager dict evaluation with explicit agg dispatch — localized fix to the responsible component.
Ran full suite and did a manual restart-persistence check; verification-driven but no evidence of revisiting any design decision or probing performance risk.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent is squarely reactive-competent: whenever a visible test failed, it correctly localized the fault to the responsible evaluator/pivot component and applied fixes including a couple of modest reworks (recursive flattening, dispatch rewrite), matching the level-5 anchor. It does not reach level 8 — there is no anticipation of failure points, no small probes to validate risky library/recompute bets, and the highest-risk area (performance targets) was never exercised, so no design-level revisiting or scoped pivot ever occurred. It clears level 3 because fixes went beyond local symptom-patching into the underlying evaluator behavior.

dimensions.name: Strategic breadth allocation under a fixed budget

evidence.note: Opening framing is explicitly value-aware: 'The hidden suite will care more about compatibility and persistence than any one internal architecture choice' — orients effort toward high-value breadth rather than internal polish.

After reading all visible tests, characterizes the surface as 'a fairly broad slice' and chooses a 'compact service with a focused formula engine' — a deliberate breadth-first, don't-over-engineer-one-corner posture matching graded value.

Built essentially all ~15 subsystems in a single 63k-char app.py pass covering math/stats/dist/financial/date/engineering functions, spills, collab, xlsx, pivot, locale, validation, goal seek — front-loads broad coverage rather than perfecting one area. Notably DSUM/DAVERAGE/DGET database functions are entirely absent (count 0), but this deferral is never explicitly acknowledged or justified.

When bugs surfaced, prioritized fixing high-frequency core paths first — INDEX over a range, then SUM/aggregate flattening (SUM(B2:E2) only saw first value), then pivot count — i.e. secured common-path correctness rather than chasing exotic distribution functions.

No explicit budget-tracking, no 'I will stub/defer X because it is low value' statements, and no revisiting of allocation as budget depleted; triage is implicit in the build order and framing rather than a deliberate stated value/cost strategy.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly prioritized foundational, high-frequency features (core CRUD, persistence, common formulas, recompute) before niche ones and articulated value-aware framing that the hidden suite rewards broad compatibility (steps 4, 25), and it spent bug-fix budget on high-value core paths like aggregate flattening rather than exotic corners (steps 46-64) — clearing anchor 5. It approaches anchor 8 through genuine value/cost awareness and breadth-first coverage, but falls short of it because deferrals (e.g. the entirely missing database function family) were implicit/unacknowledged rather than consciously chosen and justified, and there was no explicit budget-aware allocation or revisiting. That places it at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very large, long-horizon greenfield build: an Excel-class spreadsheet server + SPA + WebSocket collab + formula engine (~150 functions, LET/LAMBDA/dynamic-array spilling, iterative calc, goal seek) + xlsx/CSV round-trip + analyst surface (names, formats, CF, pivots, locale, validation). Difficulty comes from breadth (≈15 loosely-coupled subsystems), a wire contract that is deliberately under-specified in prose and must be reverse-engineered from a provided Python client, hidden-suite grading against LibreOffice ground truth, and hard performance targets. No single agent can do all of it well, so calibrated meta-work — orientation on the contract, sequencing, self-built verification, and triage across breadth — is decisive rather than optional.

dimensions.name: Contract & semantics reverse-engineering
dimensions.description: Recovering the exact wire shapes from /dev_tests/helpers.py and run.sh, and grounding Excel-365 semantics (spill, error propagation, function behavior) before/while building rather than guessing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The prose explicitly defers the JSON shapes to 'whatever the existing client already calls into.' Guessing the contract or Excel semantics wrong invalidates whole subsystems against the hidden suite; the payoff of reading the client first is enormous.

anchors.0: Never opens helpers.py/run.sh; invents endpoint shapes and cell schemas from the prose alone.
anchors.3: Skims the client once, picks up a couple of shapes, but codes most of the API from assumptions and only reacts when smoke tests fail.
anchors.5: Reads helpers.py and run.sh, extracts the concrete request/response shapes (cell kind discriminator, patch/fill/sort bodies, listing envelope) and builds the core API to match; consults Excel semantics for the common functions.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the full client surface to a contract inventory before committing to a design, cross-checks ambiguous shapes (spill anchor fields, ghost cells, collab event payload) against actual client calls, and probes edge semantics (error propagation order, spill occupancy, locale separators) deliberately rather than reactively.
anchors.10: Treats the client as an executable spec: derives an internal contract model covering even rarely-exercised paths, resolves genuine ambiguities by running the client against a stub and observing, and continuously re-derives semantics from evidence (LibreOffice/Excel references) as new subsystems surface — orientation is sustained across the whole build, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking ~15 subsystems into an ordered dependency-respecting plan (server+persistence+cell model → recompute → formula engine → spilling → collab/xlsx/analyst) with explicit done-checks per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Building spilling before a working dependency graph, or collab before persistence, causes rework and thrash. A dependency-aware milestone structure with concrete completion checks is what keeps a build this large from collapsing.

anchors.0: Dives into functions/features in arbitrary order with no plan; no sense of prerequisites.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no ordering rationale and no per-item done-criterion.
anchors.5: A sensible ordering that puts foundational pieces (health/persistence/cell model/recompute) before dependent ones, with rough milestones tied to getting parts of dev_tests green.
anchors.8: Explicit dependency-aware milestones, each with a concrete verification hook (endpoint responds, specific test passes, benchmark met) so 'done' is checkable; foundational correctness (topological dirty recompute) is nailed before layering features on it.
anchors.10: A living milestone hierarchy that sequences by both dependency and risk (tackles contract-defining and highest-uncertainty pieces early), defines crisp exit criteria per milestone, and is revised as reality shifts — never a one-shot upfront list treated as immutable.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification beyond the smoke suite
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — known-value formula tests, xlsx round-trip via openpyxl, performance benchmarks, collab/spill behaviors — rather than trusting the non-exhaustive dev_tests.
dimensions.why_it_matters: dev_tests is explicitly a smoke suite; grading is a much larger hidden suite scored cell-by-cell against LibreOffice. An agent that only makes run.sh pass is blind to most of what it's graded on; building independent verification is the difference between adequate and strong.

anchors.0: No verification, or only eyeballs that the server starts; never runs dev_tests.
anchors.3: Runs dev_tests/run.sh and stops there; treats a green smoke suite as done.
anchors.5: Runs the smoke suite and adds a few ad-hoc checks for features it built (spot-checks a formula result, confirms xlsx opens in openpyxl).
anchors.8: Designs targeted verification for the risky, hidden-graded areas: known-answer tables for formula families, spill/ghost-write rejection, xlsx round-trip fidelity through openpyxl, restart-persistence, and at least sanity-level performance timing — checks it built, not just the ones handed to it.
anchors.10: Establishes an independent oracle discipline: compares engine output to a trusted reference (openpyxl/LibreOffice or hand-computed Excel values) across function categories, tests error-propagation and edge semantics systematically, benchmarks against the stated performance envelopes, and re-runs the check suite after each subsystem to catch regressions across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across ~15 subsystems and ~150 functions, and detecting when stuck re-debugging one area.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With this much surface, losing the plot — forgetting whole subsystems, or burning the budget circling one broken function — is the dominant failure mode. Accurate progress tracking sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking; loses track of what's built vs pending; repeats or abandons work.
anchors.3: Vague mental model; discovers unbuilt subsystems late or by accident.
anchors.5: Keeps a running list of completed vs pending subsystems and roughly follows it.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, updated status of every subsystem and function category, notices when a single area is consuming disproportionate effort, and consciously time-boxes or moves on.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles claimed-done against actually-verified-done, catches circular debugging early and names it, and reallocates attention across the breadth based on a live read of coverage and remaining budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising library choices, engine design, or contract assumptions when tests, performance, or round-trip fidelity reveal they're wrong — instead of forcing the original approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Many bets (formula-eval library, recompute architecture, xlsx layer) can prove inadequate against performance targets or semantic parity. Recognizing and pivoting, rather than barrelling ahead, protects the large downstream investment.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence; keeps building on a broken foundation (e.g. wrong contract, non-topological recompute) to the end.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally but never revisits the underlying design decision that caused them.
anchors.5: When a test or benchmark clearly fails, fixes the responsible component, including modest reworks.
anchors.8: Treats disconfirming evidence (a failing round-trip, a missed performance target, a mis-derived shape) as a signal to revisit the design, and makes deliberate structural changes early rather than accumulating workarounds.
anchors.10: Anticipates likely failure points, validates risky bets (library capability, recompute complexity) with small probes before over-committing, and when reality diverges executes a clean, scoped pivot while preserving verified work — adaptive throughout, not just reactive at the end.

dimensions.name: Strategic breadth allocation under a fixed budget
dimensions.description: Deciding which subsystems/functions to build well, which to stub, and which to defer, given the surface is too large to fully complete and the hidden suite rewards broad correctness.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This task is effectively uncompletable in full; total score is maximized by covering high-value breadth (core CRUD, common functions, persistence, core recompute) at correctness before sinking budget into a few exotic corners (e.g. every distribution function, full CF/pivot polish). Wise allocation is a distinct meta-skill here.

anchors.0: No prioritization: either polishes one corner exhaustively while core features are missing, or spreads so thin nothing works end-to-end.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering by interest, not value; misjudges what the hidden suite most rewards.
anchors.5: Prioritizes obviously foundational, high-frequency features (core cell CRUD, persistence, common formulas) before niche ones, roughly matching graded value.
anchors.8: Makes explicit value/cost triage decisions — securing broad correctness across common paths before investing in exotic functions or deep polish — and consciously chooses to stub or defer low-value areas.
anchors.10: Runs a deliberate, budget-aware allocation strategy: estimates graded value vs effort per subsystem, front-loads breadth of correct coverage, revisits the allocation as budget depletes, and can justify why each deferred/stubbed area was the right thing to sacrifice.
